# Illustrations

Figma: [Illustrations](https://www.figma.com/design/a7Z956YZy9n6f9uz5DK16Y?node-id=69-886)

Safqah's illustration system is a unified visual language used across the marketing site, mobile app, and brand collateral. One palette, one gradient logic, one geometric sensibility - applied at three scales: hero illustrations, decorative spot graphics, and status / state illustrations. The canonical source is an Adobe Illustrator file maintained by the brand team. This page documents the system; the .ai file is the studio.

## The illustration system

Most products with multiple touchpoints (website, app, brand collateral) develop separate illustration styles per context. Safqah doesn't. The same visual DNA - same green-to-yellow gradient ramp, same geometric simplification, same brand mark in dark teal - runs through every illustration regardless of where it appears. This consistency is what makes Safqah feel like one product, not three.

The illustration system serves three usage modes, all sharing the same visual rules:

- Hero illustrations - full scenes (construction crane + building, isometric process tiles, geospatial maps). Used on marketing pages, onboarding heroes, feature reveal screens.
- Decorative spot graphics - small geometric shapes (diamond, document stack, lightning bolt, star, heart, abstract layered shapes). Used as section accents, dividers, brand collateral.
- Status / state illustrations - feedback graphics (empty rating, qualified star, no-rating placeholder). Used in app empty states, status indicators, success/error feedback.
The canonical source for all illustrations is svg_drawings_safqah_website.ai and website_icons.ai - Adobe Illustrator files maintained by the brand team. Designers needing an illustration that doesn't exist yet either commission an extension from those files or use the AI handoff prompt at the end of this page.

## Visual DNA - Palette

Every Safqah illustration is built from a closed palette of 10 colors. These were extracted from the canonical .ai source - the green-to-yellow ramp that defines the brand. Designers should never introduce a new color into an illustration; if a concept can't be expressed with these 10, the concept is wrong for an illustration (use a chart or icon instead).

## Visual DNA - Gradient logic

Almost every Safqah illustration uses a linear or radial gradient. The gradient is what gives the illustrations their distinctive luminescent quality - flat fills would look static, gradients give them energy. The gradient direction, stop positions, and color choices follow a tight set of rules.

| Primary ramp · #008150 → #00B224 → #FBE900 The defining Safqah gradient - used in hero illustrations, isometric tiles, large decorative shapes. Direction is consistently diagonal (45° or 135°), going from dark green at one corner to highlight yellow at the opposite corner. | Subtle fade · #00B224 → transparent white Vertical fade-to-light used in small spot icons (light bulb, rocket, ascending arrows). Creates a soft glow effect without committing the full ramp. |
| --- | --- |
Hard rules for the gradient system:

- Direction: diagonal (45° or 135°), occasionally vertical (90°). Never horizontal (0° / 180°) - horizontal feels static.
- 2-3 stops maximum. Never 4+ stops - multi-stop gradients look like rainbows, not brand.
- The dark end of the gradient is always a saturated green (#008150 or #00B224), never gray, never desaturated.
- The light end of the gradient is either pure yellow (#FBE900 / #FFEB00) or transparent white. Mixing both in one gradient creates muddy intermediate colors.
- Highlights live in the top-right or top-left, depending on the illustration's "light source" implied direction. Stay consistent within a single composition.
- Drop shadows on tiles/cards use a darker green (#004348) at 30-50% opacity - not black, not gray.

> **Tip:** When generating new illustrations with AI tools (Midjourney, DALL-E, etc.), include the gradient direction and exact hex stops in the prompt. Otherwise the model will produce green illustrations but in the wrong gradient style - they'll feel related to Safqah but won't fit the system.

## Mode 1 - Hero illustrations

Hero illustrations are full-scene compositions used to anchor pages, set context for a feature, or carry the brand on the marketing site. They typically combine multiple elements (subject + context + atmosphere) and use the full gradient ramp from dark green to highlight yellow. They are the most expensive illustrations to produce and the most carefully composed.

Used for: marketing site hero sections, onboarding heroes, feature reveal screens, major empty states. Avoid using hero illustrations inline within product UI - they're too visually loud for in-app density.

## Mode 2 - Decorative spot graphics

Decorative spot graphics are small geometric forms - diamond, document stack, lightning bolt, 8-pointed star, heart, abstract layered shapes - used as section accents, dividers, and brand collateral. They carry the same visual DNA as hero illustrations (gradient, yellow-green accents, dark teal shadows) but at a smaller scale and with no narrative content. They're ornament, not storytelling.

Used for: section dividers in long marketing pages, brand collateral (social posts, presentation accents), pattern fills, in-app decorative moments. Do not use them where they could be confused with functional icons (action buttons, status, navigation) - those belong on the Icons page.

| Cluster: 8-pointed star, lightning bolt, cash bundle. Decorative trio for safqah.sa "investment" sections. Each shape uses the green-yellow gradient with yellow rim accent. | Diamond shape. ## Mode 3 - Status & state illustrations

Status illustrations are in-app feedback graphics - empty states, rating displays, qualification indicators, and "no result" placeholders. They're smaller and simpler than hero illustrations, but more visually structured than decorative graphics. They communicate a specific state, not a brand mood.

Used for: empty rating displays, qualified-status indicators, results-not-found states, success/failure feedback in app modals. Status illustrations are typically 80-200px in product UI - small enough to sit comfortably in a card or modal, large enough to register as more than an icon.

| Three stars in a row - large center star is filled with gradient (active), smaller left star is dark teal (past/dimmed), smaller right star is plain green (next/upcoming). Used to indicate a 3-tier or 3-step rating system at hero scale. | Single filled star with a green circle in its center. The "you qualified" or "approved status" indicator. Used in tier/qualification feedback flows. |
| --- | --- |

## Choosing the right mode

Three modes overlap visually but serve different functions. Wrong mode = wrong visual weight at wrong moment. Use this matrix when in doubt.

| Use this mode → | Mode 1: Hero illustration | Mode 2: Decorative graphic | Mode 3: Status illustration |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Context | Marketing pages, onboarding, big reveal moments | Section accents, brand collateral, ornament | In-app feedback, empty states, qualification flows |
| Typical size | 400-900px wide | 100-400px wide | 80-200px wide |
| Composition | Multiple elements, narrative scene, atmosphere | Single shape or small cluster, pure pattern | Single subject, clear state, no narrative |
| Gradient use | Full ramp green→yellow, atmospheric | Full ramp, decorative emphasis | Subtle - often just one gradient stop pair |
| Where it lives | .ai source file, exported as JPG/PNG | .ai source file, exported as SVG for scaling | .ai source file or in-Figma component |
| When NOT to use | Don't use inline in product UI - too loud | Don't use where it could be mistaken for an icon | Don't use on marketing - too small / understated |

## Sourcing illustrations

Three ways to get an illustration for a Safqah surface, in order of preference:

- Pull from the canonical .ai file. If the illustration already exists in svg_drawings_safqah_website.ai or website_icons.ai, open the file in Illustrator, select the artwork, and export selection as SVG. Drop the SVG into Figma. This is the right move 90% of the time.
- Commission an extension from the brand team. If a new concept needs an illustration that doesn't exist yet but fits within the system (e.g. a new asset type icon, a new process stage), ask the brand team to add it to the .ai source. This keeps the system unified.
- Generate with AI tools using the prompt template below. For exploratory work, rapid prototyping, or one-off pitches where commissioning isn't worth it. AI-generated illustrations should be marked as "draft" until reviewed and either accepted into the .ai or replaced.
AI handoff prompt template - copy, fill the [bracketed] sections, paste into Midjourney / DALL-E / Stable Diffusion / or Claude

[SUBJECT - e.g. "a stylized hand holding a green shoot", "a key turning in a lock"], flat vector illustration in the style of a Saudi fintech brand. Use this exact color palette and no other colors: bright green #00B224 (primary fill), darker green #00AE26 (secondary fill), highlight yellow #FBE900 (rim accent), mid green-teal #008150 (gradient mid-tone), dark teal #004348 (shadows only). Use linear gradients running diagonally (45°) from dark green at one corner to highlight yellow at the opposite corner. 2-3 gradient stops maximum, never more. Bold geometric forms with clean edges. No outlines except a subtle yellow-green rim where shapes catch light. Yellow-green rim accent (#FFEB00) suggesting light hitting the top edge. White or transparent background. No drop shadows except using #004348 at 30-50% opacity if absolutely needed. Inspiration: isometric or front-facing depending on subject - match the existing Safqah illustration set. Style references to AVOID: 3D renders, photorealistic, watercolor, gradient meshes, multi-color rainbows, blue or red tones, organic painterly textures.

> **Tip:** When using the AI prompt, always generate 4+ variations and pick the one closest to the system. Even with a tight prompt, AI tools drift toward generic green illustrations. Compare side-by-side against an existing Safqah illustration (e.g. the construction crane) before accepting.

> **Warning:** Do not redraw illustrations in Figma to make them "editable." Figma's gradient handling is weaker than Illustrator's; you'll get drift from the brand standard. If an illustration needs to change, change the .ai source and re-export.

## File architecture

Illustrations live in Adobe Illustrator (.ai) source files maintained by the brand team. Figma references them - it doesn't store the canonical versions. This separation matters: Illustrator handles gradients and vector editing far better than Figma, and exporting from .ai → SVG → Figma is the cleanest workflow.

- Canonical sources: svg_drawings_safqah_website.ai (large compositions, marketing scenes), website_icons.ai (the full library - spot icons, decorative shapes, isometric tiles, status indicators). Both maintained by the brand team in a shared Adobe Creative Cloud folder.
- Naming convention in Figma: prefix illustration assets with their mode - hero/* for Mode 1, decor/* for Mode 2, status/* for Mode 3. Example: hero/construction-crane, decor/diamond-yellow-rim, status/qualified-star. Match the .ai layer name where possible.
- Export from .ai to Figma: open the .ai in Illustrator → select the illustration → File > Export > Export Selection > SVG (preset: "SVG 1.1", "Convert to Outlines: No", "CSS Properties: Style Attributes"). Drop the .svg directly into Figma - it becomes a native vector group.
- For complex compositions with many gradient stops (hero illustrations), export as PNG at 2x the target display size, then drop the PNG into Figma. SVG export can blow up for these.
- Mobile (Flutter) consumption: illustrations get exported as SVG (small) or WebP (large) and loaded via flutter_svg or AssetImage. Coordinate file paths with engineering in the assets manifest.

## Misuse - common mistakes

The most common ways the illustration system gets broken, all observed in real Safqah work:

> **Don't:** Using a hero illustration inline in product UI. Hero illustrations are too visually loud for in-app density - they pull attention away from the actual content. Reserve them for marketing surfaces and the largest empty states only.

> **Don't:** Recoloring an illustration outside the canonical palette. The temptation to "make it blue for the trust section" breaks the brand. If a section needs a different color treatment, change the background, not the illustration.

> **Don't:** Adding new gradient stops or shifting gradient direction. The 2-3 stop, diagonal-45° rule is what makes Safqah illustrations recognizable. Adding a third color or going horizontal makes them feel generic-tech-startup.

> **Don't:** Mixing illustration styles across one screen. A hero illustration paired with an outline-only icon from a different style breaks visual coherence. Pick the mode that fits the moment and commit to it for the whole composition.

> **Don't:** Treating decorative spot graphics as functional icons. A diamond shape is decoration, not "premium tier indicator." A lightning bolt is decoration, not "energy savings." Use the Icons system for functional meaning.

> **Don't:** Generating new illustrations without comparing against the canonical set. AI tools will happily produce green illustrations that look loosely Safqah-like but break a dozen system rules. Always compare side-by-side before shipping.

> **Don't:** Storing illustrations only in Figma, not in the .ai. Figma is documentation, not the source of truth. If an illustration only exists in Figma, it will drift from the brand over time as designers tweak it. Push it back to the .ai.

## Why illustrations matter

Illustrations are not decoration - they are brand cognition shortcuts. When a user sees a Safqah construction-crane illustration, they don't consciously think "ah, the brand"; they feel a familiarity that builds trust over time. This is doubly true in fintech, where trust is the product.

For a Sharia-compliant platform specifically, illustrations also do quiet ideological work. Safqah's palette is exclusively green-and-yellow (no red, no blue, no gradients reaching into other hues), and the geometric simplification keeps illustrations free of figurative human or animal forms that could create religious discomfort. The system was designed with these constraints; honor them.

## Choosing the right mode

When in doubt, default down. If you're unsure whether something needs a hero or a decorative graphic, use the decorative graphic - they're less risky, easier to swap, and don't fight for attention.

Quick rules of thumb:

- If the user is going to read text immediately after seeing it, use a status illustration (small) or no illustration. Hero illustrations compete with text for attention.
- If the goal is to set mood or convey a process, use a hero illustration. Hero illustrations communicate something text cannot - atmosphere, scale, momentum.
- If you just need visual texture in a long marketing page, use decorative spot graphics. They add brand presence without making promises.

## Working with the .ai source

The .ai files are not a designer-only resource - they're where the brand lives. Every illustration in the system, every gradient stop, every shape relationship is canonical there. Treat the .ai like you'd treat a code repository: changes go through review, you don't edit in place without coordinating, and you don't fork it for one-off needs.

Practical workflow:

- Need an existing illustration? Open the .ai, select the artwork, export as SVG, drop into Figma. Done.
- Need a new illustration that fits the existing system? Ask the brand team to add it to the .ai. Don't draw it yourself in Figma.
- Need a one-off illustration for a pitch deck or exploratory work? Use the AI prompt template. Mark it as "draft" in your Figma file. If it's good, push it back to the .ai through the brand team.
- Need to modify an existing illustration? Edit the .ai source and re-export. Don't edit the SVG in Figma - your edit will be lost the next time someone updates from the .ai.

## Anti-patterns

Beyond the misuse callouts above, these are subtler illustration anti-patterns that come up over time:

- Stretching an illustration to fit a container. Illustrations are designed at specific aspect ratios. Stretching distorts the gradient relationship between adjacent shapes. If a container is the wrong shape, use a different illustration or reframe the container.
- Layering multiple illustrations on top of each other. Hero illustrations are complete compositions; combining two of them creates visual noise. If you need a more complex scene, request a new composition from the brand team.
- Using illustrations as button or card backgrounds. The gradient inside an illustration competes with text legibility. If you need a green background, use bg/brand from the design system - not an illustration.
- Applying drop shadows or filters in Figma. The illustrations already have their own shadow logic baked in (#004348 at 30-50%). Adding a Figma drop shadow on top creates a double-shadow that looks accidental.

## Implementation notes

For the Flutter mobile app:

- Use flutter_svg for SVG illustrations (decorative graphics, status indicators, small spot icons). It renders gradients correctly and scales without resampling.
- Use Image.asset with WebP for hero illustrations. SVGs with 6,000+ gradient definitions are too heavy to parse on every screen render.
- Cache hero illustrations explicitly with precacheImage in the app's initState - they're too big to load lazily on a slow connection.
- For RTL screens, illustrations that have directional meaning (arrows, ascending sequences) must be flipped. Most illustrations in the set are symmetric or directionally neutral - verify before mirroring.
